lesson.text: Quick memory: what is a primary source? (Something made or used at the time.) Old maps, photos and street signs are primary sources about a place.
Every place has a story. Historians find it by comparing sources from different times: old maps, old photos, dates carved on buildings, and the memories of older people.
Here is the story of Millbrook, a village by a river. In 1850 it had a few farms and a water mill that ground wheat into flour.
In 1900 a railway station opened and the village grew: new houses, a school and a shop. Trains brought people, goods and jobs, so many villages grew fast when a railway came.
Names are clues! Mill Lane, Station Road and Well Street tell you what was once there, even when it has gone.
Why do places change? New ways to travel, new jobs and more people. Some old buildings are kept and some change: Millbrook's old mill is now a museum.
Try it in the world: take a photo of a spot in your world. Build something new there, then take another photo from the same place. Compare them: that is local history!

exercises.prompt: Which is the best clue about what a place was like 100 years ago?
exercises.hint: Which clue was made at that time?
choices: an old map of the place
exercises.explain: An old map was made at the time, so it shows the place as it was then.

exercises.prompt: A street called Mill Lane might tell you there was once a mill there.
exercises.hint: Street names are often chosen because of something nearby.
exercises.explain: True: many street names are clues to what was once there.

exercises.prompt: Look at the table. When did the railway come to Millbrook?
exercises.hint: Find the word railway in the table, then look at its year.
exercises.explain: The table shows the railway in 1900.

exercises.hint: Think of what is built, knocked down or changed near you.
exercises.explain: False: places change all the time, with new buildings, roads and jobs.

exercises.prompt: Put Millbrook's story in order, earliest first.
exercises.explain: Farms and a mill (1850), the railway (1900), new houses and shops (1960), the museum (today).

exercises.prompt: Why did many villages grow when a railway came?
exercises.hint: What could a train carry to and from a village?
choices: trains brought people, goods and jobs
exercises.explain: Trains brought people, goods and jobs, so more people came to live there.

exercises.prompt: Bram's grandmother remembers the village shop in 1960. What kind of source is her memory?
exercises.hint: Was she there at the time?
choices: a primary source: she was there
exercises.explain: She saw it herself, so her memory is a primary source. Historians call this oral history.

exercises.prompt: A date carved on a building's stone can tell you when it was built.
exercises.hint: Look above doors of old buildings for numbers.
exercises.explain: True: many buildings have the year they were built carved on a stone.

exercises.prompt: An old map shows a pond where there are houses today. What probably happened?
exercises.hint: Which is the most likely change over many years?
choices: the pond was filled in and houses were built
the houses sank into the pond
the map is from the future
exercises.explain: The pond was probably filled in and the land built on. Comparing maps shows changes like this.

exercises.prompt: Which question would a local historian ask about an old photo of a street?
exercises.hint: A historian wants to know about change over time.
choices: What has changed since, and why?
How can I win a race?
exercises.explain: Asking what has changed, and why, is how local historians find a place's story.

exercises.prompt: Comparing two maps of the same place from different years shows how it changed.
exercises.hint: Put an old map and a new map side by side.
exercises.explain: True: what appears or disappears between the maps shows how the place changed.

exercises.prompt: Station Road has no station today. What is the best way to check if it once had one?
exercises.hint: Which source was made at the time the station might have been there?
choices: look at an old map from 100 years ago
look at a map of another town
exercises.explain: An old map from that time would show a station if there was one.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps for finding out a place's story in order.
exercises.hint: Start with a question and finish with the story.
items: tell the story of how it changed
ask a question about the place
find old maps, photos and memories
exercises.explain: Ask a question, find sources, compare them with today, then tell the story.

exercises.prompt: Sort the sources: made at the time, or made later?
exercises.hint: Was it made when the thing happened, or long after?
exercises.explain: The 1850 map and the 1900 photo are primary sources; this year's book and the new sign came later.

exercises.prompt: Match each street name to what was once there.
exercises.hint: Each name holds a clue word.
exercises.explain: Mill Lane had a mill, Station Road a station, and Well Street a well.

exercises.prompt: Match each clue to what a historian can work out from it.
items: a pond on an old map, houses now
matches: what the shop was like then
exercises.hint: What does each clue tell you that you cannot see today?
exercises.explain: A street name can outlast what it names: a station was once there. Comparing maps shows the pond was filled in. A date stone tells when it was built. Grandma's memory is a primary source about the shop.
